title: Ostracon: Ramesses II Suckled by a Goddess

image.credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Given in honor of James N. Sherwin, Trustee 1957-1971 (1987.156)
image.license: Public domain. Released under the Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access program

altText: A flat flake of limestone with a drawing of figures on it, made in ancient Egypt. The drawing is done in lines on the stone's surface.

source.verifiedBy: Cleveland Museum of Art open-access API record (title, creator, date, medium, culture, credit line, CC0 status, description and did-you-know text)

context: An ostracon, a flake of limestone used by artisans in Thebes for practice and sketches, made during the reign of Ramesses II (c. 1279-1213 BCE) and now in the Cleveland Museum of Art. The drawing shows the king, identified as Ramesses II, suckled by a goddess. The museum adds that the artisans who carved the tombs in the cemeteries lived in a tiny community not far from their workplace.

descriptions.k: This is a flake of stone with a drawing on it. Look for the lines. Long ago in Egypt, an artist drew here. A goddess is shown looking after a young king. Can you find the two figures? Trace a line with your finger.
descriptions.g12: A long time ago in Egypt, an artist drew on a flat piece of limestone, a kind of stone. Artists used pieces like this to practice and sketch. The drawing shows a goddess caring for a young king. Look at the lines. Which ones curve, and which ones are straight?
descriptions.g35: This ostracon is a flake of limestone from ancient Egypt, made around 1279 to 1213 BCE, when Ramesses II was king. Artisans in Thebes used flakes like this to practice and sketch ideas. The drawing shows a goddess caring for the king, which may express the idea that the gods protected him. How do the artist's lines show the bond between the two figures?
descriptions.g68: This limestone flake, called an ostracon, comes from Thebes and dates to the reign of Ramesses II (about 1279-1213 BCE). Artisans used ostraca for practice and sketches. It shows the king suckled by a goddess, and he is drawn at child size even though the body is an adult's. The image may express the idea that the gods nurture and protect the king. How does the drawing's scale support that idea?
descriptions.g910: This ostracon shows Ramesses II suckled by a goddess. Ostraca were limestone flakes that artisans in Thebes used for practice and sketches, so it gives a different view from formal temple reliefs. Drawing the king at child size, though with an adult body, may be a visual way of showing divine care for the ruler. How do the drawing's scale and informal surface shape your reading of it?
descriptions.g1112: Painted on a limestone flake, this ostracon shows Ramesses II as a king suckled by a goddess, drawn at child size despite an adult body. As a practice sketch by artisans, it sits between workshop habit and royal ideology: the museum notes that those who carved the tombs lived in a small community near their workplace. How might you argue that the image expresses divine kingship, and what limits does its informal medium place on that claim?

k.daily: Look at the stone. What do you see drawn on it?
k.emotion: How does this old drawing make you feel? Pick a feeling word.
k.observation: Point to the figures in the drawing. How many can you find?
k.analysis: Which figure looks bigger and which looks smaller? Point to each.
k.line: Trace one line of the drawing in the air. Does it curve or go straight?
k.shape: Find a shape in the drawing, such as a curve or a circle. Point to it.
k.color: What colors do you see in the lines and in the stone?
k.texture: This drawing is on a stone. How would the flake feel if you touched it?
k.space: The stone is flat. Where on the stone did the artist put the figures?
k.light: Which part of the stone looks lightest to you? Point to it.
k.meaning: A goddess is looking after a young king. Who looks after you?
k.culture: This was made in Egypt long, long ago. What would you like to know about the person who drew it?
k.technique: The artist drew on a piece of stone. What other things could you draw on?
k.personal: If you could draw a picture on a stone, what would you draw?
k.critical: Why might an artist practice a drawing before making a bigger one?

g12.daily: Why might an artist draw a goddess and a king together?
g12.emotion: What feeling do you get from the two figures standing close together? What shows it?
g12.observation: Look for one minute. Which lines or small parts did you not see at first?
g12.analysis: How can you tell which figure is the goddess and which is the king? What clues help?
g12.line: Trace the outline of one figure with your eyes. Where do the lines curve and where do they bend?
g12.shape: What shapes make up the body of one figure? Draw one of them in the air.
g12.color: Which colors are used for the drawing, and how do they look against the stone?
g12.texture: The drawing is on limestone. How might the stone feel different from paper?
g12.space: How did the artist fit the figures onto a small, flat stone? What do you notice about where they sit?
g12.light: Look at the stone's surface. Where does it look lighter or darker, and why might that be?
g12.meaning: A goddess cares for the young king. What does that show about how Egyptians thought of their gods?
g12.culture: Artists in Thebes used stones to practice. Why would they use stone instead of paper?
g12.technique: The artist used lines made with paint. What do you think it was like to draw on rough stone?
g12.personal: What would you practice drawing over and over, and why?
g12.critical: Why might it matter that this is a sketch and not a finished carving?

g35.daily: What details of the drawing show you who the important figures are?
g35.emotion: What mood does the scene of a goddess caring for a king create, and which details help create it?
g35.observation: Choose one figure and describe its pose, its outline and what it seems to be doing.
g35.analysis: How does the artist arrange the two figures to show which is the protector and which is the king?
g35.line: How do the artist's lines show the outlines and shapes of the figures, and where do they seem quick or careful?
g35.shape: How does the artist use the figures' shapes to suggest age, size or importance?
g35.color: How does the contrast between the painted lines and the stone help you read the figures?
g35.texture: How might the stone's surface have changed the way the artist drew and painted on it?
g35.space: The king is drawn small next to the goddess. How does scale tell us about their relationship?
g35.light: How might the lighter and darker parts of the stone surface affect how clearly you see the drawing?
g35.meaning: The scene shows a goddess caring for a king. What might it say about how Egyptians thought the gods looked after rulers?
g35.culture: Artisans who carved tombs lived in a small community near their work. What might that tell you about who made this sketch?
g35.technique: Why might artisans use limestone flakes for practice and sketches rather than finished walls?
g35.personal: What would you want to ask an artisan who made practice sketches for royal images?
g35.critical: How is a quick sketch on stone different from a carved temple relief, and why might that matter when we study it?

g68.daily: How does the drawing communicate the relationship between the goddess and the king? Use details you can see.
g68.emotion: What tone does the intimate scene of care create, and how does that contrast with the idea of a powerful king?
g68.observation: What do the quality and confidence of the lines suggest about the artist's training?
g68.analysis: How does the artist organize the two figures on the small flake to focus attention on their connection?
g68.line: How do contour lines define the figures, and where might the line quality show speed or careful control?
g68.shape: How does drawing the king at child size while keeping an adult's body change how you read the figure's shape and meaning?
g68.color: How do the pigment and the limestone work together to make the drawing legible?
g68.texture: How might the irregular limestone surface have affected the drawing, and what traces of that can you see?
g68.space: How does scale create a hierarchy between the goddess and the king in this small, shallow space?
g68.light: How do tonal differences in the stone and in the pigment help the figures stand out or recede?
g68.meaning: The king is suckled by a goddess. What idea about kingship and divine support might this image express?
g68.culture: How might a sketch made by artisans in a workers' community differ from images made for a temple or royal tomb?
g68.technique: What does the use of painted limestone flakes tell us about workshop practice in New Kingdom Thebes?
g68.personal: What role do imagery and symbols play in how leaders today are presented as supported or protected?
g68.critical: What can we know for certain from this object, and what do we have to infer about its purpose?

g910.daily: How does the ostracon use a simple scene to express a larger idea about kingship? Cite specific visual evidence.
g910.emotion: How does the contrast between the king's youthful scale and adult body create a particular tone, and how does that shape interpretation?
g910.observation: Examine how line is used to define the figures. What does it reveal about the artist's skill and the conventions of Egyptian drawing?
g910.analysis: How does the arrangement of the figures establish their relationship, and which visual choices create hierarchy?
g910.line: How do the artist's contour lines balance convention with individual handling, and what might that suggest about workshop practice?
g910.shape: How does depicting Ramesses II at child size with an adult body work as a visual convention, and what might it communicate?
g910.color: How does the limited contrast between pigment and stone support clarity, and how does it differ from monumental painting?
g910.texture: How does the use of an irregular limestone flake as a drawing surface affect both the making and the meaning of the work?
g910.space: How does the compression of figures into a small flake shape the viewer's sense of intimacy compared with a large wall relief?
g910.light: How might the tonal range of stone and pigment guide the viewer's eye through the composition?
g910.meaning: How might an image of a goddess suckling the king reflect broader ideas about divine legitimacy in New Kingdom Egypt?
g910.culture: How does knowing that tomb artisans lived in a small community near their workplace change how you think about who made and used this sketch?
g910.technique: What can a practice sketch reveal about workshop training and methods that a finished monument cannot?
g910.personal: Where do you see visual messages of legitimacy and care in the public images of leaders you know?
g910.critical: What are the challenges of drawing conclusions about royal ideology from a single informal sketch, and what would strengthen your argument?

g1112.daily: How does this sketch condense a complex theology of kingship into a few lines? Support your argument with visual evidence.
g1112.emotion: How does the tension between intimacy and royal status shape the emotional register of the image, and how would you argue for your reading?
g1112.observation: Look at the junctions of line and surface. What do they reveal about the pace, confidence and conventions of the draughtsman?
g1112.analysis: How does the composition position nurture as a form of authority, and how does hierarchy operate despite the closeness of the figures?
g1112.line: How does the linear economy of the drawing reflect both training in a set canon and the freedom of an informal medium?
g1112.shape: How might the combination of child-scale and adult body function symbolically rather than naturalistically, and how would you test that reading?
g1112.color: How does the relationship between pigment and limestone affect legibility, and what does that suggest about the status of the object?
g1112.texture: How does the use of a discarded stone flake complicate hierarchies of material, making the work both humble and ideologically charged?
g1112.space: How does the small, shallow field concentrate meaning in contrast to monumental programs, and what does that imply about audience?
g1112.light: How do the stone's natural tonal variations interact with the drawn line, and does the artist seem to exploit or ignore them?
g1112.meaning: How might the image of a suckling goddess operate as both religious doctrine and political message, and how would you weigh the evidence?
g1112.culture: What does the setting of a workers' community near the tombs suggest about the circulation of royal imagery among those who produced it?
g1112.technique: How might a practice sketch complicate the assumption that Egyptian art was rigidly formulaic, and how would you evaluate that claim?
g1112.personal: How does your own view of authority and care shape the way you respond to an image that joins them?
g1112.critical: What would a careful argument look like that this is a rehearsal for a formal work rather than a self-contained image, and what evidence would it need?

safety.method: SENSITIVE ASPECT FOR REVIEWER: the title and subject show a goddess suckling (nursing) the young king Ramesses II. Per the age-appropriate rule, K-grade 5 text and questions avoid the word nursing and focus on line, drawing on stone, practice sketches and the idea of a goddess caring for and protecting the king; the nursing is stated plainly and factually only from grade 6 up. Title, date, culture, medium (painted limestone), credit line, CC0 licence status and the museum's description were read from the Cleveland Museum of Art open-access API summary. The image file was not viewed; a person should view the image, confirm how the figures are shown and approve it before release.

teacherNote.context: An ostracon (a limestone flake) from Thebes, made in the reign of Ramesses II (c. 1279-1213 BCE). The Cleveland Museum of Art explains that ostraca were used by artisans for practice and sketches, and that this one shows the king suckled by a goddess, drawn at child size despite an adult body. The scene may express the idea that gods nurture and protect the king. For younger students, focus on line, materials and the idea of a caring goddess.
directions: Have students draw a quick sketch with a pencil or marker on a flat stone or heavy paper, and compare practice sketches with finished work.
Ask older students to describe the drawing in neutral terms, then discuss what the scene may have meant for ideas about kingship.
Discuss why a rough stone flake might survive as evidence of how artisans worked.
